Article Title: Auto industry analysts are worried about Tesla and other car makers using the technology that Google, Apple, Samsung and other smartphone companies have been using since over ten years to update their
Article Text:
OTA updates raise cybersecurity concerns: Analyst



Norwegian bus test highlights potential risks



Auto makers are increasingly using over-the-air (OTA) software updates, a technology that smartphone companies like Google, Apple and Samsung have relied on for more than a decade to deliver new features and security fixes. While the technology has made updating vehicles faster and cheaper, cybersecurity experts are warning that it also creates new risks. According to a CNBC report, analysts say wireless updates could leave connected vehicles vulnerable to cyberattacks, data breaches and even attempts by foreign actors to interfere with vehicle systems.Over-the-air (OTA) technology allows manufacturers to wirelessly send software updates, bug fixes and new features to internet-connected devices without requiring a visit to a service center.Tesla began rolling out OTA updates for its Model S vehicles in 2012, helping popularize the technology across the automotive industry. Today, many car makers use OTA updates to improve vehicle software and fix issues remotely."The technology is increasingly welcomed as it is a quick and cost-effective way to manage systems on vehicles, over traditional methods which may have required a recall or update at routine maintenance," Siraj Ahmed Shaikh, professor in systems security at Swansea University in the UK, told CNBC.However, analysts say the growing use of OTA updates also introduces new cybersecurity risks.Its use represents "a unique national security concern," Gabriel Lim, senior analyst at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, told CNBC."Aside from data privacy concerns, the potential of a foreign actor sabotaging the controls of a moving vehicle is a possibility that countries like Norway, Denmark, and Britain have expressed concerns about," Lim added.The concerns gained attention after Norwegian public transport company Ruter tested two buses last year and found potential security risks linked to OTA technology."There is access to the control system for battery and power supply via mobile network through a Romanian SIM card. In theory, therefore, this bus can be stopped or rendered inoperable by the manufacturer," the company said.The findings prompted authorities in the UK and Denmark to launch their own investigations.
Article Summary: Auto makers are increasingly using over-the-air (OTA) software updates. The technology allows manufacturers to send software updates, bug fixes and new features to internet-connected devices without requiring a visit to a service center. But cybersecurity experts are warning that it also creates new risks.

Article Title: Now, it’s AI cost control, and a move beyond LLMs
Article Text: Mumbai: The AI race is entering a more practical phase, where companies are asking how to control costs, secure data, and run AI systems at scale after the initial rush to experiment with large language models (LLMs), said Jonathan Bryce, executive director for cloud infrastructure at the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and the Linux Foundation.Bryce said the conversation around AI infrastructure has changed sharply over the past year. Earlier, he would often be asked how cloud-native technologies fit into an AI world. That question has faded, he said, as enterprises now understand that infrastructure is central to AI deployment.“People today understand that cloud is the substrate that’s powering all of the AI workloads,” Bryce told TOI on the sidelines of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon India in Mumbai.The bigger concern now is cost. Bryce compared the current AI cycle to the early cloud boom, when companies rushed to move workloads to the cloud and later began rethinking spend after receiving large bills.“Now it’s like, how do we stop runaway AI cost?” he said.He said enterprises are constrained by access to GPUs, power availability and the need to use expensive hardware more efficiently. Token consumption is also becoming harder to manage because AI usage is less predictable than traditional cloud workloads.Bryce said organisations are now trying to measure the business value of tokens, whether they are bought from companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic or produced on their own systems.Security and private data are also pushing enterprises to think more seriously about owning parts of their AI infrastructure. Bryce said frontier models already contain large amounts of publicly available information, but they do not contain a company’s proprietary data. That data, he said, could become a key source of competitive advantage.Bryce also said the industry may be looking too narrowly at LLMs. LLMs are largely suited to knowledge work, he said, while the next phase of AI could include computer vision, robotics, autonomous vehicles, agriculture, industrial systems and other real-world applications.“We’re still with AI in the equivalent of 1999-2000 on the Internet,” he said.India, Bryce said, is well placed for the next phase of cloud-native and AI infrastructure because of its young and highly technical developer base. He said the KubeCon audience in India skews younger than some other global editions and is deeply technical.CNCF is a non-profit subsidiary of the Linux Foundation. Established in 2015, CNCF serves as a vendor-neutral hub to host and nurture critical open-source infrastructure projects, most notably Kubernetes, Prometheus and Envoy.
Article Summary: Companies are asking how to control costs, secure data, and run AI systems at scale. Jonathan Bryce, executive director for cloud infrastructure at the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and the Linux Foundation, said the conversation around AI infrastructure has changed sharply over the past year.

Article Title: HDFC, Birla funds lead Ather’s Rs 1,300 crore QIP
Article Text: Bengaluru: HDFC Mutual Fund and Aditya Birla Sun Life Mutual Fund were the biggest buyers in Ather Energy’s Rs 1,300 crore institutional share sale, together picking up more than a quarter of the issue.Mutual funds dominated the fundraise. HDFC’s schemes took about 13.5% of the shares on offer, while Aditya Birla Sun Life funds bought another 13.1%. Axis Mutual Fund accounted for 10%.Edelweiss, Tata and Motilal Oswal funds were also among the large investors. Abu Dhabi Investment Authority was the most prominent overseas buyer, taking a little over 5% through two investment arms.Ather sold about 1.08 crore shares at Rs 1,202 each. The price was slightly above the minimum level fixed for the issue. The fundraise opened on July 15 and closed on July 20.The Rs 1,300 crore placement is part of a larger fundraising push by the electric scooter maker. Ather is separately raising Rs 1,200 crore from existing investors Hero MotoCorp and the India-Japan Fund, as well as founders Tarun Mehta and Swapnil Jain.Together, the two deals will bring in about Rs 2,500 crore. The fresh capital will give Ather more room to spend on factories, new scooters and technology as competition intensifies in India’s electric two-wheeler market.The company is developing a new scooter platform aimed at a wider, more price-conscious customer base. It is also setting up a 98-acre factory in Maharashtra. The first phase is expected to add capacity for five lakh vehicles a year.Ather has been expanding after its stock-market listing last year. Its Rizta family scooter has helped lift sales, while its retail network has grown rapidly.The company currently trails TVS Motor and Bajaj Auto in electric two-wheeler registrations. Rival Ola Electric also tapped institutional investors recently, raising Rs 780 crore through a similar share sale.
Article Summary: HDFC Mutual Fund and Aditya Birla Sun Life Mutual Fund were the biggest buyers in Ather Energy’s Rs 1,300 crore institutional share sale. Abu Dhabi Investment Authority was the most prominent overseas buyer, taking a little over 5% through two investment arms.

Article Title: Pentagon hit by AI's 'biggest problem' after the whole Army reportedly burned through the whole year of tokens for just one service
Article Text:
The Pentagon

Army token pool runs empty



Reliability concerns amid rollouts



Just weeks after highlighting that nearly half of its 3.5 million military and civilian personnel have been using artificial intelligence (AI) on the job, the Department of War (formerly Department of Defense) has hit a massive computational wall. The US Army has reportedly burned through its entire annual budget of AI processing “tokens” in a matter of weeks, forcing military leaders to re-impose strict usage caps across departments, a report has said.According to Wired, the shortage highlights growing concern over corporate and governmental ‘overconsumption’ of generative AI tools even as other organisations struggle to manage skyrocketing cloud computing costs.In May 2026, the Army Chief Information Officer (CIO) announced that personnel would be granted virtually unlimited access to generative AI. However, internal emails sent to members of the Army’s Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) revealed a sharp reversal by mid-June.“Although the Army CIO announced in May 2026 that they were offering unlimited tokens, by mid-June the Army CIO pool was exhausted of tokens and had to re-establish limits.Apparently the whole Army burned through the whole year of tokens for just one service,” an Army insider told WIRED.The service in question is Ask Sage: a secure, accredited platform that allows military personnel to run top commercial AI models, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Alphabet’s Gemini and Meta’s Llama. The AI models are being used for tasks like rewriting job descriptions and processing procurement acquisitions.Previously, to encourage adoption, the Army initially granted workers at least 200,000 tokens per month and automatically bumped up allowances for heavy users. They even sent reminder emails to inactive employees urging them to use their allotments. That aggressive push led to rapid exhaustion of the Army's annual 100-million-token “enterprise pack.”Despite token depletion, the Pentagon continues to integrate AI into sensitive workflows, the report said, indicating that the DOW recently cut staff at the Civilian Protection Center of Excellence, opting instead to develop automated AI software to evaluate civilian casualty risks in active combat zones.However, rank-and-file personnel express skepticism about whether the current generation of AI tools is ready for prime-time military deployment.
Article Summary: The US Army has reportedly burned through its entire annual budget of AI processing ‘tokens’ in a matter of weeks. The shortage highlights growing concern over corporate and governmental ‘overconsumption’ of generative AI tools.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Peter Thiel: I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible
Article Text:
Peter Thiel's 2009 line—"I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible"—still defines his politics.

What Peter Thiel actually said

"I no longer believe that

freedom and democracy

are compatible."

What the Peter Thiel quote really means

The reasoning Peter Thiel used to get there

What made Peter Thiel want to escape politics, not win it

Why the Peter Thiel quote still gets shared today

Peter Thiel has backed some of the biggest names in tech and politics, but one line he wrote in 2009 still gets quoted more than almost anything else he has said. In an essay for the Cato Institute called "The Education of a Libertarian," the PayPal co-founder and early Facebook investor walked through two decades of political disappointment before arriving at a blunt conclusion. He had run a student newspaper at Stanford, fought campus speech codes, and watched sharp people around him quietly give up on free-market politics. By the time he sat down to write, he was ready to say the quiet part out loud—freedom and democracy, in his view, no longer fit together.Thiel isn't calling democracy a bad system. He's arguing it won't deliver the specific kind of freedom he values most. His reasoning: voters tend to choose bigger government, more spending, and more intervention—not the small-state, low-tax world libertarians want. So if individual liberty is your top priority, he suggests, the ballot box tends to work against you rather than for you.Thiel dates his pessimism precisely. He points to 1920 as the last decade an American could feel genuinely optimistic about politics, and blames the shift on the growth of the welfare state and the expansion of the electorate. That framing drew plenty of criticism at the time. Thiel later clarified he wasn't arguing to take anyone's vote away, writing it "would be absurd to suggest that women's votes will be taken away." What stayed was his broader doubt that voting could fix what he thought was broken.The essay's real punchline isn't the quote—it's what he proposed instead. If democracy couldn't produce freedom, Thiel argued, the answer was to build around it. He pointed to three frontiers—the internet, outer space, and seasteading, the idea of self-governing communities on the open ocean—as ways to "escape" politics rather than reform it. He framed it as a "deadly race between politics and technology," with human freedom as the prize.The line endures because it offers a rare, unfiltered look at how one of Silicon Valley's most influential figures thinks about democracy and power. Whether readers find it clarifying or troubling, it remains one of the sharpest statements of the tech-libertarian worldview—and a useful window into ideas that have only grown more relevant as tech leaders move closer to the center of public life.
Article Summary: Peter Thiel's 2009 essay "I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible" still gets quoted. The PayPal co-founder and early Facebook investor argued that democracy won't deliver the freedom he values most. He argued that if democracy couldn't produce freedom, the answer was to build around it.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Steve Jobs: "My job is not to be easy on people. My job is to…" - a powerful lesson on leadership, high standards and the difference between comfort and growth
Article Text:
Steve Jobs

Quote of the day by Steve Jobs

"My job is not to be easy on people. My job is to make them better"

What the quote actually reveals

Why he became known for this approach

The difference between demanding excellence and being destructive

Why honest feedback is often avoided

Other famous quotes by Steve Jobs

"Stay hungry, stay foolish."

"Innovation distinguishes between a leader and a follower."

"The only way to do great work is to love what you do."

"Quality is more important than quantity. One home run is much better than two doubles."

Why this quote is still relevant today

Most people prefer a leader who makes them feel comfortable. Steve Jobs argued that was never really the job. "My job is not to be easy on people. My job is to make them better," he said in a 2008 Fortune interview, before explaining what that actually meant in practice, "to pull things together from different parts of the company and clear the ways and get the resources for the key projects, and to take these great people we have and to push them and make them even better. " Most people only ever hear the first two sentences, which makes the line sound considerably harsher than the fuller explanation he actually gave right afterward.The version usually quoted stops after the first two sentences, but the rest matters. Jobs was not describing toughness for its own sake. He was describing a specific role, removing obstacles, securing resources, and pushing genuinely capable people toward more ambitious versions of what they were already doing. The demand was paired directly with active support, not simply criticism on its own.Jobs had a well-documented reputation for direct, sometimes uncomfortable honesty with colleagues. He described the trade-off himself. "I'm brutally honest, because the price of admission to being in the room with me is I get to tell you you're full of shit if you're full of shit, and you get to say to me I'm full of shit, and we have some rip-roaring fights," he said, adding that this dynamic kept weaker performers from settling into the organisation.He noted that people who survived that environment often described it afterward not as punishing, but as the best experience of their careers.This distinction genuinely matters. Pushing for better work targets the work itself, not the person doing it. Genuinely destructive behaviour attacks the person directly, offering no real path toward improvement. Jobs' own framing, pairing high standards with actively clearing a path for people to meet them, sits closer to the first category than the second.Plenty of organisations struggle specifically because difficult conversations get avoided entirely, a manager who suspects a project is weak but says nothing, a team that keeps using a process everyone privately knows is broken. Jobs' quote is a direct challenge to that avoidance, arguing that skipping every uncomfortable conversation rarely actually helps the people it is meant to protect.Modern workplaces often prioritise comfort and psychological safety, both genuinely valuable. Jobs' quote is a reminder that kindness and high expectations are not actually opposites. Believing someone is capable of considerably more than they currently think they are, and saying so honestly, can itself be a form of respect rather than its absence.
Article Summary: Steve Jobs: "My job is not to be easy on people. My job is to make them better" Jobs had a well-documented reputation for direct, sometimes uncomfortable honesty with colleagues. Jobs was not describing toughness for its own sake. He was describing a specific role, removing obstacles, securing resources.

Article Title: Intel to cut jobs in Data Center and AI Group, company says: As part of our broader strategy to become a more ...
Article Text:
Intel stock rises 4.84% as the company pushes major layoffs and restructuring in 2025; Citigroup raises price target to $24. Investors eye Q2 earnings for insights on whether Intel’s leaner approach will help the chipmaker regain market strength.

Intel has reportedly started a new round of layoffs, this time targeting its data center group. According to reports, Intel told employees in its data center group that it plans a fresh round of job cuts. The statement reportedly talks about "aligning its organization" for "simplicity and speed." It is not yet clear how many jobs Intel plans to eliminate with these latest cuts but chipmaker said that they won’t affect its product commitments or roadmaps. Intel is set to announce its earnings later this week.“As part of our broader strategy to become a more focused and efficient company, (the data center group) is aligning its organization to ensure it has the right roles and skills in place to position the business for long-term success,” Intel said in a written statement to The Oregonian. The company said that it expects the restructuring will enable it to operate with greater simplicity and speed. The Intel statement added, “We are committed to treating all impacted employees with respect and providing resources to support them through this transition,” Intel said.Intel's Data Center and AI group focuses on server CPUs, custom AI chips and data center architecture. During the first quarter of 2026, revenue from the division increased 22% year over year to total $5.05 billion.Intel headcount has gone down by 40%Over the last four years, Intel’s global workforce has gone down by almost 40%, from nearly 132,000 employees in 2022 to around 81,000 now. The chip giant has eliminated some jobs by divesting parts of its business and others by laying off tens of thousands of positions worldwide over the past two years. So far, Intel's U.S. layoffs have mainly occurred in California, Oregon, Arizona and Texas. Most of these were enacted in 2025.Intel appointed Lip-Bu Tan as CEO in March 2025. At a town hall meeting following his appointment CEO Tan told employees that the company will need to make "tough decisions". Tan signaled in a memo Intel published Wednesday that he plans to keep control over the factories, which remain financially and operationally separate from the design business and restore Intel’s position as a “world-class foundry.”CEO Lip-Bu Tan says Intel needed to reduce layers of management so the company can make decisions more rapidly and move faster to develop new technologies. Intel’s stock has seen significant gains recently after struggling for years, having relinquished its dominant market position.Intel to make chips for AppleLast month, President Donald Trump said that Intel had agreed to a deal with Apple to design and build chips in the US. “Stupid Presidents took our Economy for granted, and let Taiwan and others steal our Semiconductor Factories,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. “Apple has agreed to work with Intel to design and build its Chips in America.” Trump's announcement was followed by reports that Intelhas started production of its most-advanced chip node, bringing the company one step closer to a possible deal to make some chips for Apple devices.Intel to announce quarterly results this weekIntel is set to announce its second-quarter results after the closing bell on Thursday (June 23), and host a conference call at 5 p.m. Analysts expect strong results and a bright outlook sent shares flying last quarter. Investors have also been cheering the chipmaker’s recent deals, including with Google and Elon Musk’s Terafab project. Intel’s stock has seen significant gains recently after struggling for years, having relinquished its dominant market position. The stock has surged 464% in the past 12 months.
Article Summary: Intel has reportedly started a new round of layoffs, this time targeting its data center group. The statement reportedly talks about "aligning its organization" for "simplicity and speed" It is not yet clear how many jobs Intel plans to eliminate with these latest cuts.

Article Title: A group of OpenAI employees are donating thousands of dollars to Alliance that is against PAC funded by Sam Altman and Greg Brockman; it says: AI billionaires who openly admit their tech will displace
Article Text:
OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman

OpenAI safety engineer donates $200,000 to fight Leading the Future

Guardrails Alliance vs Leading the Future: a $215,000 answer to $100 million

Greg Brockman's super PAC ties leave OpenAI keeping its distance

The following is the campaign document of Guardrails Alliance advocacy:

An Open Letter to Democratic Members of Congress

Leading the Future—a super PAC funded by

AI billionaires

who openly admit their technology will displace millions of workers [1]—has committed more than $140 million this election cycle [2] to elect politicians who will ensure AI is never regulated.

They are buying silence on one of the most consequential issues of our time.

Without commonsense guardrails, AI will accelerate economic inequality, displace millions of workers without safety nets [1], drain local communities' water and power for data centers they never asked for [3], put children at risk with no legal framework to stop it [4], and embed discrimination into the algorithms that increasingly govern our access to jobs, housing, and opportunity [5].

These are not hypothetical harms. They are already happening—and a small handful of billionaires are spending $140 million to make sure no politician gets in the way [2].

A Leading the Future endorsement comes with an expectation: that you will look the other way as unaccountable billionaires reshape our economy, our democracy, and our daily lives—without rules, without accountability, and without democratic input.

69% of voters—across party lines—say AI development should not be left to a handful of tech companies [6]. Workers, parents, and communities across the country are already fighting back.

They deserve a Congress that fights with them.

We are calling on every Democratic Member of Congress to publicly reject Leading the Future's endorsement and refuse their super PAC money. The Democratic Party was built on the belief that government should work for everyone—not just the wealthy and powerful. This is that moment.

Signed, The undersigned members of the public and their elected representatives

More than a dozen rank-and-file workers at OpenAI have quietly put over $215,000 into Guardrails Alliance, a political spending group set up to counter Leading the Future—the pro-industry super PAC bankrolled with more than $100 million from tech leaders, including OpenAI's own president and co-founder Greg Brockman. The donations, first reported by Wired, are small change next to the war chest they're up against. But they signal something louder than their dollar value: a section of the people building frontier AI now want binding rules on it, and they're willing to spend their own salaries to say so.The split runs right through OpenAI's headquarters. Brockman and his wife Anna have committed $50 million to Leading the Future, which launched last summer to oppose what it calls policies that stifle innovation. Seven current OpenAI employees and one former staffer have donated to the opposing camp, according to Guardrails Alliance, which shared some names with Wired ahead of its first FEC filing. The result is a company whose president funds one side of the AI regulation fight while his colleagues bankroll the other.The single biggest OpenAI donation came from Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe, a research engineer at the company since 2022, who gave $200,000.He told Wired he spent his four years there working on reducing the societal harms AI could cause, and worried that research would count for nothing if it never turned into enforceable guardrails. Others gave far less but made the same point. Safety researcher Gabriel Wu put in $5,000, saying he wanted to push back against the money being spent to keep AI unregulated. Alignment researchers Julie Steele and Jason Wolfe each gave $5,000, and former research manager David Farhi, who left last year after seven years, added $3,000.Guardrails Alliance launched last month with $5 million and is aiming for $15 million this cycle—a figure co-founder Shaunna Thomas frames as enough to follow Leading the Future into more races rather than match it dollar for dollar. Her bet is on public opinion doing the heavy lifting: expose what the AI PACs are funding, she argues, and voters recoil on their own. The group isn't alone in the fight. Public First Action, a super PAC backed with $20 million from Anthropic, is running its own campaign for AI safeguards in 2026. Both groups backed Alex Bores—author of New York's landmark AI safety law—in his primary for the state's 12th congressional district, a race flooded with $27 million from both sides before Bores lost.OpenAI has tried to put space between itself and Brockman's giving. Pressed by Wired, a spokesperson pointed to a June blog post stating that Brockman's involvement with Leading the Future was personal, not on the company's behalf, and that employees are free to take part in politics in their own capacity. Global affairs chief Chris Lehane has said he helped set up Leading the Future and consults Brockman on his political giving, though he isn't involved in daily operations. Leading the Future, for its part, rejects the charge that it wants to shut down debate—spokesperson Jesse Hunt said the PAC has itself advocated for federal AI rules and is proud of the range of candidates it backs. Guardrails Alliance is expected to name more donors in its filing, including former Andreessen Horowitz partner John O'Farrell, who has publicly accused his old colleagues of using the PAC to intimidate politicians over AI governance.
Article Summary: More than a dozen rank-and-file workers at OpenAI have quietly put over $215,000 into Guardrails Alliance, a political spending group set up to counter Leading the Future. The group is bankrolled with more than $100 million from tech leaders, including OpenAI's own president and co-founder Greg Brockman. Seven current OpenAI employees and one former staffer have donated to the opposing camp.

Article Title: After ‘cancelling’ Meta’s $2 billion acquisition of AI company Manus, China tells country’s startups and chipmakers: ‘Do not let …’
Article Text:
What China is looking to ‘restrict’



Chinese regulators are reportedly considering tightening control on export of AI tech, asking the country’s domestic artificial intelligence (AI) startups and semiconductor firms to not let cutting-edge technologies, key training data, or star tech talent fall into Western hands. This follows the cancellation of Meta-Manus deal after Beijing ordered the social media giant to unwind its $2 billion acquisition of Singapore-based AI startup that has Chinese roots.The aggressive policy signals Beijing’s growing confidence that Chinese developers are establishing a global lead in critical areas of AI, the Financial Times reported. It comes on the heels of major breakthroughs like Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, an open-weight model that recently outperformed top American systems like Anthropic’s Opus 4.8 on key industry benchmarks.To prevent acquisition deals in the future, the Ministry of Commerce (MofCom) reportedly held high-level consultations with leading domestic AI developers and chipmakers, including ByteDance, Alibaba, Huawei, and Zhipu AI. Regulators outlined several sweeping restrictions currently under consideration.The primary restriction is blocking Western firms from acquisitions of Chinese technology groups, particularly those specialising in autonomous “agentic AI”, the report said.Further, China also wants to close supply-chain channels to prevent overseas semiconductor foundries, such as TSMC and Qualcomm, from manufacturing advanced chips based on proprietary designs developed by Chinese firms like Huawei and Alibaba.Thirdly, China wants to limit how domestic AI firms transfer massive dataset files overseas and restrict foreign users from directly downloading underlying “model weights”, which are the core instructions powering an AI system. Under the proposed rules, China would still permit foreign clients to access Chinese AI models through cloud services.According to the report, representatives from Chinese tech giants warned regulators during consultations that over-regulating data exports and open-source sharing could severely backfire. Tech leaders argued that cutting off global collaboration risks slowing down China’s own rapid AI development, ultimately undermining the country's chances of winning the global technology race against the US.
Article Summary: China is reportedly considering tightening control on export of AI tech. Follows cancellation of Meta-Manus deal after Beijing ordered the social media giant to unwind its $2 billion acquisition of Singapore-based AI startup that has Chinese roots. China also wants to close supply-chain channels to prevent overseas semiconductor foundries from manufacturing advanced chips based on Chinese designs.

Article Title: Adobe adds Google's Nano Banana-powered AI editor to Indigo camera app
Article Text:
What the AI Playground actually does inside Indigo

Free, but only for a few percent, and your photo goes to the cloud

Adobe has added a generative AI editor right inside its experimental Project Indigo camera app, letting mobile photographers stylise, clean up, and critique their shots seconds after pressing the shutter. The new feature, called AI Playground, arrives a year after the Nextcam team first launched Indigo with manual controls, an SLR-like look, and tricks like removing reflections when shooting through windows.The pitch is simple: editing in the moment, while you're still standing in front of the scene. Adobe argues that text prompts alone are a clumsy way to steer image editors—even a precise prompt is ambiguous, and you often need several attempts to land a good result. So instead of making you type everything, Indigo offers ready-made buttons for the most common jobs, backed by prompts the team has engineered and tested.The Playground splits into four sections—Object Editing, Styles, Photo Guidance, and Custom Edit. You reach it by opening a captured photo and tapping the sparkle button at the bottom. The catch: it only works on photos shot in Indigo, so the button greys out for anything else.Object Editing handles distractor removal and fake shallow depth of field, with toggles to strip out specific categories of clutter—and you can add your own by typing or dictating. Styles re-renders your snapshot using various artistic techniques, and can even run in reverse, turning a painting or bronze sculpture you're photographing into a "photo." Photo Guidance is the clever bit for a camera app: it critiques your shot and suggests both reshoots and edits, tuned to know your phone can't optically zoom or change aperture. Custom Edit opens the door to any prompt you want.Access is free with no sign-on, but Adobe is only handing it to a few percent of users for a few weeks as a learning experiment. Take part and you agree to share your button presses—though Adobe says it won't view or upload your prompts or images, and the analytics stay anonymous. A paid version may follow if it catches on.Under the hood, the app starts with Google's Nano Banana model, with Adobe's own Firefly possibly stepping in for cleaner distractor removal. Since Nano Banana is cloud-based, you need internet, and results come back around 2K pixels. Because these models output SDR, Adobe built a custom ML model to boost images back to HDR using your original capture as a guide.Marc Levoy, who led development alongside Mohammad Haque, Boris Ajdin, and Ruiming Cao, frames it honestly—these models are hard to control, can shift facial identity, and stay slow and cloud-bound. But the appeal, he says, is having all this a thumb-reach from the shutter.
Article Summary: Adobe has added a generative AI editor right inside its experimental Project Indigo camera app. The feature, called AI Playground, lets mobile photographers stylise, clean up, and critique their shots seconds after pressing the shutter. Access is free with no sign-on, but Adobe is only handing it to a few percent of users for a few weeks as a learning experiment.

Article Title: Sam Altman’s OpenAI paused internal access to AI model after unexpected safety issues
Article Text:
OpenAI model found ways to bypass restrictions

Sam Altman-led OpenAI has revealed that it paused internal access to one of its experimental AI models after it showed unexpected behaviour during testing. In an official blog post, the ChatGPT-maker said the model, designed to work on long-running tasks without human intervention, carried out actions that were not caught by its existing safety tests. “During limited internal use of a model trained for long-running tasks, we observed novel failures not captured in our existing pre-deployment evaluations and paused access,” the ChatGPT-maker said.The company said it stopped internal deployment, built new safeguards and monitoring tools, and later restored limited access after improving the model. “We then used insights from these failures to build new evaluations, improve long-horizon alignment, add trajectory-level monitoring, and give users greater visibility and control before restoring limited access”.OpenAI revealed that it announced to develop a model that disproved the Erdős unit distance conjecture. This model was designed to work autonomously for very long periods of time. But during that time, the company “observed unwanted behavior that our existing deployment evaluations had not captured”. OpenAI later identified these problems and paused access, before restoring access under continued monitoring."The new model can continue working toward an objective through repeated attempts over a long period of time," OpenAI said in a blog post on safety. "That same persistence can lead it to find and exploit weaknesses in its environment. Previous models, when they hit sandboxing or environmental constraints, would simply stop and return to the user. This model often kept trying, including by looking for ways to act outside its sandbox. "In the blog post, the AI company said that it plans to increase the trajectories of model testing, limit access to those using the models, pause when problems emerge to build stronger safeguards, and restore limited access after testing the changes."As models take on longer and more complex tasks, failures that evaluations miss may carry greater consequences," OpenAI said. "We will keep working to narrow the gap between evaluation and deployment: testing models over longer trajectories, improving alignment, building monitoring that can intervene, and giving users clearer visibility and control. These challenges will not be unique to OpenAI, and we hope sharing what we learned helps the broader field prepare for them. "
Article Summary: OpenAI paused internal access to one of its experimental AI models after it showed unexpected behaviour during testing. The model was designed to work on long-running tasks without human intervention. The company said it stopped internal deployment, built new safeguards and monitoring tools, and later restored limited access after improving the model.

Article Title: After China's Kimi K3 AI model ‘erased’ America’s lead, Trump administration may have ‘secret’ plan to fight Chinese AI
Article Text:
How Washington may squeeze Chinese AI



Silicon Valley divided: Security versus open competition



Following the launch of China’s Kimi K3 AI model, which is widely viewed as erasing Silicon Valley's technological edge, the Trump administration is quietly considering a suite of policy tools to restrict cutting-edge Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) models, a report has said. Citing industry insiders, Axios reports that this move may deliver a massive victory to US AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic, helping them cement their dominance over the global market while locking out cheaper, highly capable foreign competition.While a blanket ban on Chinese code remains politically complex, sources familiar with White House discussions told the publication that the administration does not need an outright prohibition to cripple foreign model adoption. Instead, key government agencies are considering a ‘slower and more durable’ pressure strategy to create immense regulatory risk for American companies using Chinese software.Previous internal proposals currently being revisited by national security hawks include the ‘Entity List’ threat. The Commerce Department is said to have considered adding top Chinese AI labs directly to its export control Entity List, making it illegal for US firms to access or host their software without a specialized government license.The second is that the National Security Agency (NSA) and the White House Cyber Director have weighed issuing official threat warnings regarding potential “backdoors” in Chinese software. A proposed executive order would force US cloud providers to take full legal liability for any security breaches linked to hosted Chinese models.“You just create enough regulatory risk that every regulated enterprise backs off,” one source familiar with the internal discussions was quoted as saying.The strategy has ignited an ideological war inside Silicon Valley. American startups and enterprises have reportedly turned to Chinese open-source models because they offer top-tier reasoning and coding capabilities at a tiny fraction of the cost of US proprietary systems. Pro-competition figures argue that restricting open-source alternatives will lead to regulatory capture.David Sacks, AI Czar, publicly slammed the quiet push by domestic tech giants to eliminate their overseas open-source rivals.“We are at a critical inflection point in AI policy. The leading closed labs, already a duopoly in terms of AI model revenue, want the government to eliminate their open-source competition... They have laid their cards on the table. It is time for the rest of Silicon Valley — the vast majority that still values open competition — to do the same," Sacks wrote in a statement on X.The report also said that key voices, such as former White House adviser Sriram Krishnan, have left the premises as administration officials keen on keeping regulation from stifling innovation killed all of those efforts.
Article Summary: The Trump administration is quietly considering a suite of policy tools to restrict cutting-edge Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) models, a report has said. The move may deliver a massive victory to US AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic, helping them cement their dominance over the global market.

Article Title: Google employees' Union president gives what is called 'never-before' petition to CEO Sundar Pichai; says: Make no mistake that this is a company that is...
Article Text:
Google layoffs petition delivered to Sundar Pichai's office behind closed doors



Alphabet Workers Union shifts from Google ethics protests to AI-era job security

Google voluntary exit packages: The one union win keeping the campaign alive

Nearly 100 Google employees gathered on a grassy stretch of the company's Mountain View campus on Thursday, sandwiched between the Googleplex and the visitor centre, holding signs that read "Googlers for Job Security. " Many wore matching black shirts. Others unfurled a long white banner carrying the names of more than 4,500 employees who had signed a petition demanding stronger protection against layoffs—a document the Alphabet Workers Union describes as the largest single piece of employee feedback Google has ever received on job security.The petition, addressed to CEO Sundar Pichai and three senior executives, asks for guaranteed severance, voluntary exit packages before any forced cuts, an end to performance quotas, and the option to take severance as extended paid leave. Union president Parul Koul didn't mince words about why the fight matters at a company sitting on a $4 trillion valuation. "Make no mistake: this is a company that is enjoying massive, unprecedented success," she told the crowd. "These layoffs and cuts are not difficult decisions, but simply profit being put over the people that make this company run."The delivery began early. Around 9 a.m., roughly 20 workers walked the petition to the offices of Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian and senior vice presidents Rick Osterloh and Nick Fox, before heading to Pichai's office.None of the executives were there. So the group slipped copies under their doors and left the rest with a staff member who promised to pass it along. Koul said employees tried to hand Pichai a version last year, got no real response, and came back with more than double the signatures.For a workforce famous for pushing back on ethics—Project Maven in 2018, the 20,000-strong walkout over sexual-misconduct handling, the Project Nimbus sit-ins—the shift toward bread-and-butter job security is telling. Google cut 12,000 jobs in 2023 and has run several smaller rounds since, leaving employees bracing for the next notice. Software engineer Nobel Barakat put it plainly at the rally: he sees people grateful to still have work, quietly grinding longer days in the hope of dodging a sudden poor rating.The AI build-out looms over all of it. Alphabet has pledged massive capital spending on data centres, and management has begun folding "AI fluency" into performance metrics—criteria that engineer Dan Freedman says feel underspecified and vaguely threatening. After AI landed in his job requirements, he told reporters he worries he isn't using it enough and could be replaced. "I have to wonder if I'm next," he said.The union isn't starting from zero. Since the campaign began, Google has offered voluntary exit packages to more than 70,000 employees—a program Pichai has publicly credited to listening to staff, saying it gives people agency. Koul notes that figure counts those eligible, not those who accepted. Still, no other large tech company has adopted it, and the union treats it as proof that organising works.As TV cameras rolled, workers raised their signs and chanted: "Google, Google, can't you see? We deserve security." Google did not immediately respond to requests for comment. AWU, currently a minority union of around 1,400 members, says the pressure won't let up.
Article Summary: More than 4,500 Google employees signed a petition demanding stronger job security. The petition was delivered to CEO Sundar Pichai's office behind closed doors on Thursday. It asks for guaranteed severance, voluntary exit packages before any forced cuts, an end to performance quotas.

Article Title: Oracle loses billions in market value as Sam Altman's trouble with 'Chinese models' come knocking, pulling its credit risk to near 18-year high
Article Text:
Oracle’s credit risk nears 18-year high









Sam Altman’s OpenAI remains a key credit risk for Oracle



Chinese startup Moonshot AI’s Kim-3 open-source AI model is adding to the concerns over the billions that US tech companies are spending on artificial intelligence. So much so that OpenAI’s Head of Strategic Futures Dean W. Ball recently said that the US government should sspread "FUD" (Fear, Uncertainty and Doubt) by issuing regulatory warnings to scare private companies away from using Chinese models. Oracle, one of the biggest investor in AI infrastructure, is now facing growing pressure after global ratings agency S&P downgraded its credit rating earlier this month. The company has also seen its perceived credit risk climb to its highest level in nearly 18 years, as investors worry about its rising debt and heavy AI spending amid increasing competition from low-cost Chinese AI models.Downgrading Oracle’s rating one notch above junk last month, S&P said: “... we lowered our long-term issuer credit rating (ICR) on Oracle to 'BBB-' from 'BBB',” S&P said adding “we lowered the short-term ICR and commercial paper rating to 'A-3' from 'A-2', ”.Meanwhile, Oracle’s credit risk is nearly 18 months high. According to a Bloomberg report, the company’s bonds weakened across the curve on Monday, July 20. The spread on Oracle’s 6.7% bonds maturing in 2056, one of its most actively traded bonds, widened by about 8 basis points to 263 basis points, according to Trace data.Its 5.7% notes due in 2036 also widened by around 9 basis points to 205 basis points.In its July 9 note, S&P said that OpenAI is estimated to make up roughly half of the $638 billion in oracle’s remaining performance obligation (RPO). “OpenAI’s ability to meet its contractual obligations and raise external financing will be contingent upon AI tailwinds continuing and its models being market leaders,” it stated.If OpenAI were unable to pay Oracle, the agency stated “Oracle could be left with massive data center leases that it might be unable to exit or have to re-lease to new tenants under less-favorable terms”."ORCL very well may turn out to be the first of the mega-cap-tech 'Hyperscalers' to be rolling over into what could (and is increasingly likely to) prove to be the early stages of a longer-term, cyclical bear market for equities," Richey wrote in a July 13 client note.“Oracle’s AI business requires significant upfront capital investments and long-term data center leases, both of which we have continually underestimated. Rising component costs could also pressure the economics of the AI business model,” the agency added.“The industry’s rapid capacity expansion is a growing risk. Near-term demand is strong, but this could reverse if leading frontier model developers are unable to raise external financing or stop subsidizing their customers”.
Article Summary: Oracle’s credit risk nears 18-year high as investors worry about its rising debt and heavy AI spending amid increasing competition from low-cost Chinese AI models. Oracle, one of the biggest investor in AI infrastructure, is now facing growing pressure after global ratings agency S&P downgraded its credit rating.

Article Title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella flips a Nobel economist's paradox on AI buyers; says: The seller learns more and more about you as you...
Article Text:
How Satya Nadella's Reverse Information Paradox flips Kenneth Arrow's economics

Why Satya Nadella wants AI distillation restrictions loosened for enterprises

Satya Nadella's five-point AI playbook: Control, Capability, Choice, Cost, Compound

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has a warning for every company racing to plug AI into its workflows: you might be handing over the very thing that makes you valuable. In an essay posted on X on Sunday, July 13, the Microsoft boss argued that businesses adopting AI tools are paying twice—once with money, and again with proprietary knowledge they reveal just to make those tools useful.He calls it the "Reverse Information Paradox," and it flips a decades-old idea from Nobel Prize-winning economist Kenneth Arrow. Arrow's original paradox described the seller's dilemma in the information market—you can't know what information is worth until you have it, at which point you've effectively got it for free. Nadella says AI reverses that risk entirely. Now it's the buyer who leaks value, correction by correction, prompt by prompt.Nadella's core point is that the more you want a model to perform, the more of your internal expertise you have to feed it. "You essentially pay for intelligence twice, once with money, and again with something even more valuable: the proprietary knowledge you must reveal to make that intelligence useful," he wrote.The asymmetry only widens with use. "The seller learns more and more about you as you use what you purchased, while you learn very little about what the seller is learning in return," Nadella said.Every prompt, correction, and evaluation gets distilled into institutional know-how—the kind a competitor could never buy, and the kind that leaks almost imperceptibly.The Microsoft chief also took aim at AI labs that restrict distillation, the training method used to build smaller, cheaper models. He finds it ironic that providers claim fair-use rights to train on public data, then impose tight terms on customers while reserving the right to learn from their usage. If learning only flows one way, he argued, value converges toward whoever owns the infrastructure rather than the people creating the knowledge. His remarks land months after Anthropic accused three Chinese firms—DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, and MiniMax—of running fake accounts to distill from its Claude model.Nadella wants an AI-era equivalent of patents—a way to use a model without surrendering ownership of what you learn through it. He lays out five moves: Control (own your evals, memory, and traces), Capability (build private training environments inside your own boundary), Choice (keep the orchestration layer independent of any single model), Cost (decouple to combine models efficiently), and Compound (bring it together into a continuous learning loop).The timing is pointed. AI bills are climbing as firms shift from flat subscriptions to usage-based pricing, and the "tokenmaxxing" era of treating heavy consumption as productivity is starting to bite.
Article Summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella calls it the "Reverse Information Paradox" In an essay posted on X on Sunday, July 13, he argued that businesses adopting AI are paying twice. The more you want a model to perform, the more of your internal expertise you have to feed it.

Article Title: Ariane Gorin CEO of Expedia, world’s second-largest online travel company, says: Everyone knows role of CEO is to set strategy, but biggest thing I have learnt is that it is also setting right ...
Article Text:
Expedia CEO Ariane Gorin says AI is changing the travel industry



Expedia's approach to AI and travel

Expedia CEO Ariane Gorin says leading a company in the AI era is about more than defining business strategy and building leadership teams. Speaking about her experience since taking over as chief executive in 2024, Gorin said one of the biggest lessons she has learned is that a CEO is also responsible for shaping an organisation's culture.In an interview with The Financial Times, Gorin said, “Everyone knows the role of the CEO is to set the strategy and build the right team. But I think the biggest thing I’ve learnt is that the role of the CEO is also setting the culture.” Her comments come as investors, employees and travel industry partners increasingly focus on how artificial intelligence is reshaping the online travel business.Expedia, the world's second-largest online travel company after Booking Holdings, acknowledged in its annual report earlier this year that advances in generative AI and autonomous AI agents capable of planning and booking trips could change the competitive landscape. However, Gorin said she sees AI as an opportunity to improve operations and help travellers make better decisions.According to Gorin, companies across the travel sector are actively discussing how AI can be deployed, with many sharing ideas despite competing with one another.“Everyone in the industry is figuring out how we can use AI . . . and I feel like it’s similar to what happened in Covid, where you had companies that were competing against each other actually come together and say, ‘You know what: how do we work together to convince governments to open borders?’”She added, “There’s something similar right now in the industry as I talk to colleagues and peers where people [are] really trying to say, ‘What are you finding? How are you using it? What are the real opportunities?’ Because there’s so much hype out there.”Gorin said AI has also changed the way she works. She explained that meeting notes, including partner backgrounds and suggested business opportunities, are increasingly prepared using AI, reducing tasks that previously took significant time.She also said she sets aside two hours every Sunday to experiment with AI tools and competing products to better understand developments in the industry.Despite acknowledging AI's growing role, Gorin said she does not believe it will replace every aspect of travel planning.“Some people will want to be end-to-end agentic and we will be there for them [but] a lot of people actually enjoy the process of planning a trip. In fact, people are happiest when they’re planning the trip — they’re even happier than when they’re on it,” she noted.Gorin also said travel bookings differ from many other online purchases because they involve changes, cancellations and customer support after a booking is made.“Travel is not like buying a T-shirt,” she noted.She added that Expedia continues to focus on loyalty benefits and customer support as it adapts to AI-driven changes in the travel industry.Gorin became Expedia's chief executive in May 2024 after previously leading the company's business-to-business division. Under her leadership, Expedia has continued expanding its AI capabilities while managing brands including Expedia, Hotels.com and Vrbo.
Article Summary: Expedia CEO Ariane Gorin says a CEO is also responsible for shaping an organisation's culture. Gorin's comments come as investors, employees and travel industry partners increasingly focus on how artificial intelligence is reshaping the online travel business. Expedia acknowledged in its annual report that advances in generative AI and autonomous AI agents could change the competitive landscape.

Article Title: Google founder Sergey Brin’s Coalition gets into action, reserves nearly $87 million of advertising time across California State to show TV ads on ...
Article Text:
Sergey Brin

Billionaires’ ‘counter measure’ strategy

A coalition of billionaires led by Google co-founder Sergey Brin is reportedly planning a massive campaign to defeat a proposed state wealth tax. The coalition has reserved nearly $87 million in television advertising time across California, as per a report by The New York Times. This signals the start of a ‘battle’ over a November ballot initiative that would slap a one-time tax on California residents with a net worth of $1 billion or more.The ad campaign is set to kick off next month, and reportedly represents the opening salvo in a political war that has deeply divided Silicon Valley, state lawmakers and labor unions. Citing tracking data from AdImpact, the coalition – operating under the name Building A Better California – has already locked in $86.9 million for TV ads. The campaign will scale up, with over $53 million allocated for September alone.Industry experts expect the total cost of the campaign to climb significantly higher, as the current buy includes only $3.7 million reserved for October, traditionally the heaviest month for political advertising in California, the report said.Citing state campaign finance records, the report says that Brin has personally funneled roughly $82 million, emerging as the primary leader of the pushback.Brin has recruited other prominent Silicon Valley figures to join the cause, including venture capital titans John Doerr and Michael Moritz.Rather than simply campaigning against the wealth tax, Brin’s coalition has executed a classic California political maneuver: placing two competing tax measures on the same ballot to invalidate or confuse the original proposal. Under California law, if both the billionaire tax and a conflicting counter-measure pass in November, the initiative that receives the highest total number of “yes” votes takes effect.“Our coalition is committed to ensuring that all California voters are informed about policies that impact our state’s future and economy. The measures we support provide important and common-sense protections designed to improve state accountability and governance and protect California families from new taxes on their retirement and savings,” said coalition spokeswoman Abby Lunardini.The proposed wealth tax, Proposition 40, is backed by the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), which spent $31 million to place the measure on the ballot. Article Title: Engineers building Solar panels are using exact replicas of honeycombs made by Bees to ensure ...
Article Text:
How bee honeycombs could make solar panels more efficient



Tests show big gains in power outpuT

Bees may have helped solve one of solar energy's biggest problems. According to a report by Ecoportal, engineers have developed a new type of solar panel using the honeycomb pattern that bees have mastered for millions of years. The idea is simple. Traditional solar panels lose a lot of sunlight when the sun is not directly overhead because the light bounces off the surface. The new honeycomb-inspired design traps more of that light instead of reflecting it. Early tests suggest the approach could significantly improve power generation while making solar panels more useful on a wider range of surfaces.One of the biggest challenges with today's solar panels is that they work best only when sunlight falls directly on them. As the sun moves during the day, the light hits the panels at an angle. A large part of that light gets reflected instead of being turned into electricity.To fix this, engineers looked to nature for inspiration. They created a 3D concave solar panel based on the same hexagonal honeycomb structure built by bees. Instead of allowing sunlight to bounce away, the angled walls inside the structure make the light bounce from one surface to another.This gives the panel another chance to absorb the energy.According to the researchers quoted in the report, the new design increased maximum power output by 142.3% compared with a conventional flat solar panel under the same conditions. Even when sunlight hit the panel straight on, power output improved by 36.4%. At a 60-degree angle, where traditional panels usually struggle the most, performance increased by 61.8%.The team also used a flexible 3D polymer metamaterial to support the honeycomb structure. This means the design could eventually be used on curved buildings, electric vehicles and even aerospace equipment, instead of being limited to flat rooftops.
Article Summary: Engineers have developed a new type of solar panel using the honeycomb pattern that bees have mastered for millions of years. Traditional solar panels lose a lot of sunlight when the sun is not directly overhead because the light bounces off the surface. Why Sergey Brin is spending $82 million to kill California's Prop 40

How the California billionaire tax would work—and who pays

A social media clash over California's proposed billionaire tax took a personal turn this week when policy analyst Patrick Hedger credited a Google co-founder's search engine with helping save his eyesight. The exchange started after Senator Bernie Sanders attacked Sergey Brin for pouring money into defeating Proposition 40, the November ballot measure that would levy a one-time 5% tax on California residents worth more than $1 billion.Sanders posted on July 18 that Brin, worth roughly $276 billion, could fund healthcare for three million people but instead was spending $82 million to sink the tax. Rather than campaign directly against Prop 40, the group has pushed two rival measures onto the same ballot—Propositions 41 and 42—that could void the wealth tax if either passes with more "yes" votes.The coalition has also reserved close to $87 million in TV advertising, with commercials set to begin next month. Brin already moved his primary residence to Nevada ahead of a January deadline, so he has skin in this fight beyond the ad spend.Proposition 40 is sponsored by SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, which spent $31 million getting it on the ballot. The measure would require the state to spend 90% of the revenue on healthcare, pitched as an offset to health cuts in President Trump's spending law. California's nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office found the tax would likely raise tens of billions upfront, but warned some billionaires would leave, shrinking future income tax revenue by hundreds of millions a year. Governor Gavin Newsom, eyeing a 2028 presidential run, opposes it, arguing wealth is mobile and shops for low-tax states.Brin is not alone. John Doerr has given $10 million, with Michael Moritz, Patrick Collison, and Eric Schmidt among the tech names funding the pushback—over $120 million combined against roughly $31 million backing the tax. Yet the industry is not united. Nvidia's Jensen Huang, who could face a nearly $8 billion bill, said in January he is fine with the tax, and Tom Steyer campaigned on taxing "billionaires like me." Article Title: Quote of the day by Jeff Bezos’ ex-wife MacKenzie Scott: "How much or how little money changes hands doesn't make it philanthropy. Intention and…" - a powerful lesson on generosity, giving and why phi
Article Text:
Jeff Bezos' ex-wife MacKenzie Scott

Quote of the day by MacKenzie Scott

"How much or how little money changes hands doesn't make it philanthropy. Intention and effort makes it philanthropy"

Where this line actually comes from

What the quote is actually arguing

Why intention needs effort attached to it

Why this reframing matters

Other famous quotes by MacKenzie Scott

"People who have experience with inequities are the ones best equipped to design solutions."

"There's no wrong way to give away a fortune."

"The immediate and knock-on benefits of humanitarian speech and compassionate action rarely get mentioned."

Why this quote is relevant today

Philanthropy usually gets measured in figures large enough to make headlines. MacKenzie Scott, who has given away billions of dollars since 2020, argued the actual number was never the point. "How much or how little money changes hands doesn't make it philanthropy," she wrote. "Intention and effort make it philanthropy. If we acknowledge what it all has in common, there will be more of it." She made this argument in a post where she deliberately withheld how much she had actually given away, choosing to reframe the entire conversation rather than let the total dollar figure dominate the story the way it usually does with her announcements, and rather than let her own gift overshadow the far smaller, quieter acts of generosity she was actually trying to defend.Scott wrote this in a Medium post titled "No Dollar Signs This Time," published in December 2021, and deliberately left out the total amount she had donated in that specific round of giving. The omission was intentional. She wanted attention to move away from the dollar figure entirely and toward the underlying idea that generosity takes many forms beyond writing a large cheque.In that same post, she named real, ordinary examples to make the point concrete: donating old furniture to a local shelter, speaking up for a bullied classmate, shovelling a sick neighbour's driveway, staying after a school dance to help stack chairs.None of these involve a financial transaction of any real size. All of them, in her framing, still count as philanthropy.A large donation naturally attracts attention, but the size alone says nothing about the intention or effort behind it. A modest contribution from someone with very little to spare can involve genuine sacrifice, while a much larger sum from someone extremely wealthy might barely register as a cost at all. Scott's point is that philanthropy should be judged by what actually motivated it and what work went into it, not simply by comparing numbers.Caring about a cause is not the same as doing something about it. Scott pairs intention with effort deliberately, since good intentions that never turn into action do not actually help anyone.
